---
title: "Bitmask: Encode a Set as One Integer"
description: "Memorisable mathematical reasoning with small numerical examples."
---

## When to recognise the pattern

When n is small and state includes a subset of used items.

## The key question

**Why does checking one bit answer whether an element belongs to the chosen subset?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
\operatorname{has}(m,i)=(m\ \&\ 2^i)\ne0
$$

**Every symbol explained:** m is a nonnegative integer bitmask; i is a zero-based element index; 2^i sets exactly bit i; & is bitwise AND; ≠0 means this bit is selected.

**Substitute actual numbers:** For mask m=5, binary 101, test i=2: 5&4=4 ≠0, so element 2 is selected. Test i=1: 5&2=0, so element 1 is absent. Thus selected indices are {0,2}.

## Why this is mathematically correct

The binary representation is a sum of distinct powers of two. An AND with 2^i isolates the coefficient of that power; nonzero means the corresponding subset element exists.

## Limits and counterexamples

Number of possible subsets of n items is 2^n. Bitmasks do not remove exponential state count; they make state representation and transitions compact. Fixed-width signed integers need care for large shifts.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: Set membership is one bit; add with OR, remove with AND complement, enumerate subsets only when n permits 2^n states.**

Now reproduce the equation, example and proof aloud, without looking.

**Interview problems:** Travelling Salesperson DP; Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets.
